title: Small loads. A monumental block.
subtitle: Carry the ingredients. Form the block where it will stay.
summary: Follow the idea behind Davidovits’ limestone demonstrations: prepare a workable mixture, carry it in portions, pack a timber form, and let it harden.
sceneDescription: A pale limestone block cast inside a wooden form on a masonry course, with a mixing basin, a moving basket, and a narrow approach.
modelNote: A simplified sequence inspired by modern re-agglomerated limestone demonstrations. Timing, dimensions, and handling are illustrative.

steps.name: Prepare
steps.title: Start with the right raw material.
steps.text: Davidovits’ demonstrations use disaggregated limestone and a binder mixture. Choosing suitable material is part of the proposal, not an incidental detail.

steps.name: Carry
steps.title: Move portions through the available space.
steps.text: A basket can pass through a route too narrow for the finished block. The same total mass still has to arrive, along with any water and binder.

steps.name: Pack
steps.title: Build up the block inside its form.
steps.text: The mixture is placed and compacted. This scene emphasizes packing a workable mix rather than treating it as a freely flowing modern concrete.

steps.name: Cure
steps.title: Allow time for a load-bearing stone.
steps.text: The block remains supported while it develops strength. Real curing times, water demand, and construction throughput require measurements.

steps.name: Strip
steps.title: Take away the boards.
steps.text: The finished block is already on its course. Casting in place could reduce the final heavy-lifting operation, while leaving an ingredient-supply problem to solve.

issues.title: Moving a very large stone
issues.mechanism: Breaking delivery into small loads avoids transporting the completed block as one object.
issues.remaining: Casting does not remove mass, lifting work, mixing labor, or the need to obtain suitable ingredients.

issues.title: A distant quarry
issues.mechanism: If suitable local inputs exist, a cast block could use them. If its aggregate comes from a distant quarry, that material still needs transport.
issues.remaining: A quarry match and a transport distance must be evaluated for the particular block; distance alone is not evidence of casting.

issues.title: A finished object wider than its entrance
issues.mechanism: Formwork and small loads could enter separately and be assembled inside.
issues.remaining: The object's date, installation sequence, chemistry, and available workspace must support that scenario.

hypothesis: Joseph Davidovits proposes that some Egyptian blocks were made from re-agglomerated limestone. Modern demonstrations establish a stone-making possibility; identifying ancient examples is a separate materials question.
alternative: Quarried masonry, transported with organized labor and lifting systems, is the conventional account. Petrographic comparisons have also challenged the casting interpretation.
test: Track the complete work needed for a specified block: sourcing, ingredient transport, water, mixing, mold reuse, curing, and strength. Compare both the logistics and the microstructure with the relevant quarried stone.
